newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FEATURE - Moves to weaken EU competition powers face defeat.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Moves to weaken EU competition powers face defeat.

text.p: European Union heavyweights France and Germany have put forward proposals which some independent experts fear would weaken the European Commission's wide powers to ensure free competition.

While they look set to be rejected, the proposals highlight a running debate over exactly what role the EU's Brussels-based executive should play in fighting anti-competitive business practices and liberalising the bloc's industries.

Germany wants to take powers away from the Commission and hand them to an independent cartel agency, while France seeks to amend an EU treaty provision giving the Commission power to dismantle state monopolies.
Bonn and Paris have introduced their suggestions separately to an inter-governmental conference (IGC) that aims to propose EU treaty reforms to EU leaders at a summit in Amsterdam on June 16 and 17.
The two countries have different views on competition policy and market liberalisation, with Germany generally taking a more free-market approach.
But experts say both initiatives, while different in purpose, could dilute some of the Commission's authority.
"They are both proposals that would actually take power away from the Commission," said Alec Burnside, senior partner at the Brussels branch of law firm Linklaters & Paines.

Competition policy experts say the chances that the texts will be agreed are slim because they would have to win approval from all 15 EU countries. Most other member countries seem content to leave the Commission's competition powers intact.

But any change in the Commission's role would be crucial for businesses across Europe since the EU executive has wide-ranging authority in the competition field. It can issue orders to end state monopolies, impose heavy fines on price-fixing cartels and block corporate mergers it considers anti-competitive.
GERMAN PROPOSAL WOULD HIT EU COMPETITION POWERS
The German proposal would directly hit the Commission's powers in vetting mergers and cartels.

Germany's powerful cartel office, Bundeskartellamt, last year stepped up a longstanding campaign to transfer some of the Commission's powers to an independent agency. It says the present system leaves EU officials open to political influence.
Last year, Bonn asked the IGC to endorse treaty language to allow a cartel agency to be created.
EU Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert has fiercely attacked the idea, saying the agency was not needed and was not likely to be more efficient or independent than the Commission.
Burnside agreed that such a body might be no more independent than the Commission.

"Inevitably, it is going to have representatives of the 15 member states, there are going to be the same sort of problems that (the Commission's competition division) and the Commission face transferred to another forum."

He advocated a more transparent system which would be less vulnerable to political influence, however, saying an independent competition agency was fundamentally a good idea but the time was not yet ripe.
Apart from some initial Italian support, however, the idea has failed to win backing from other member states. "Germany is on its own," one EU official said.
The possible impact of the French proposal is less clear-cut, but some competition experts say it would water down the controversial article 90 of the EU treaty.

That article requires governments to apply EU competition rules to public companies and operators awarded special or exclusive rights "in so far as the application of such rules does not obstruct the performance...of the particular tasks assigned to them".
It also empowers the Commission to take action on its own to crack open state monopolies. "It is quite an essential tool for the development of competition," one EU official said.

He cited the telecommunications sector, where the Commission has issued a series of "Article 90 directives" to abolish a range of restrictions and to enforce a January 1, 1998 deadline for complete liberalisation.
FRANCE SEEKS TO SHIFT EMPHASIS TO PUBLIC SERVICES
However, France has long objected to the Commission's use of article 90, even challenging it unsuccessfully in the EU court.
Now Paris wants to amend the article, saying in its official proposal that too often the EU had given the impression "that it is indifferent or even hostile to public services".

For example, it wants the treaty to ensure that EU rules are applied to public utilities in a way that takes account of "the conditions under which they act and the constraints to which they are subjected."

Experts say the proposal reflects French fears that far-reaching liberalisation could interfere with the state's traditional role of ensuring that services such as electricity and water are provided to all consumers at an affordable price.
The issue is especially sensitive in France in view of several public sector strikes in the last few years.
"What they want to do, I would say, is to weaken it and shift the emphasis from competition to public services," said Stephen Kinsella, managing partner in the law firm Herbert Smith.
The Commission, as would be expected, opposes changing the article, saying it already strikes a balance between national public service objectives and EU liberalisation goals.
"There is a clear-cut, unanimous consent not to touch article 90," one Commission official said.
Instead, it has suggested listing "a contribution to the promotion of services of general interest" as a Union activity elsewhere in the treaty.

UNICE, the European employers' group, also opposes a change. "We quite frankly believe the balance (between public services and competition policy) is there. Why change it?" said UNICE director Fiona Marcq.
Other countries, especially those that are ahead in opening their markets, share the fear that the new language could be used in the EU court to slow down liberalisation.
"We have at least suspicious, if not negative, views on ideas of amending article 90 on public services," said Finnish EU ambassador Antti Satuli.
Burnside said the French proposal, if adopted, would "be a serious step back for the liberalisation initiatives which have made painfully slow progress over the years."
But Kinsella at Herbert Smith doubted that the French proposal would have much impact even if it were adopted. "It is still terribly vague...I don't think it would do it," he said.
